body_sections.heading: What you kept coming back to
body_sections.prose:
Three times across the exercises you described the same thing in different words: work that outlasts the person who commissioned it. You said it about a staircase, about a client who came back after nine years, and about the reason you refuse to subcontract the finish carpentry.

That repetition is the finding. You did not name durability as a value. You kept telling stories in which durability was the point, which is stronger evidence than naming it would have been.

body_sections.heading: The refusal that came first
body_sections.prose:
Before you could say what the brand was, you said what it was not. Not a flipper. Not a volume builder. Not the company that finishes on time by finishing badly.

A brand that knows its refusals before its promises is unusual and it is an advantage. The refusals are specific enough to act on, which is why they carry the positioning in the section after this one.

always: Name the material and where it came from
never: Promise a date you have not checked
Use a stock photograph of someone else's work
Compete on price against a volume builder

body_sections.heading: The register
body_sections.prose:
Warm, heavy, quiet. Everything you described had weight to it: oiled walnut, cold morning air in a framed-out room, the particular silence of a house before the drywall goes in.

Nothing you described was bright, fast or loud. That absence is as useful as the presence, because it rules out most of what the category does.

body_sections.heading: Material before colour
body_sections.prose:
Every sensory word you produced was a material word. Oiled, cold, heavy, grain, dust. Not one was a colour word, and not one was a mood word of the kind the category leans on.

That matters because it tells the visual work where to start. A brand whose senses are material should not be styled from a mood board of colours. It should be built from the surfaces it already names.

body_sections.heading: What the register rules out
body_sections.prose:
Bright, fast and loud are all out, and so is the entire vocabulary of speed. You never once described work as quick, efficient or streamlined, and when asked directly about turnaround you talked about sequence rather than duration.

That is a differentiator hiding in a silence. Most of the category sells speed. You cannot, and you should stop apologising for it.

body_sections.heading: Why this palette and not the obvious one
body_sections.prose:
The category default is charcoal and safety orange, which reads as contractor rather than maker. Your sensescape pointed at material colour instead: the colours of the things you build with, not the colours of the equipment you build with.

So the palette is drawn from oiled wood, cold light and unfinished steel. It rules out the orange, and ruling that out is most of the differentiation.

body_sections.heading: The position, and what it costs
body_sections.prose:
You sit between the architect-led firms who win on drawings and the volume builders who win on price. Neither is beatable on their own ground and you should stop trying.

The ground you can hold is the one neither wants: the client who has already been let down once and now cares more about being told the truth than about being told what they want to hear. That client is slower to find and far slower to lose.

body_sections.heading: The three you are actually measured against
body_sections.prose:
Not the national builders. In every story you told, the comparison was local and specific: the architect-led studio two towns over, the volume outfit that underbid you in spring, and the client's own brother-in-law who once built a deck.

Those three set the real frame. The first beats you on drawings, the second on price, the third on trust. Only the third is winnable on their own ground, and it is winnable by being the one who says what will go wrong before it does.

body_sections.heading: What you give up
body_sections.prose:
Holding this position costs you the fast jobs and the clients who want to be told yes. That is a real cost and it will feel like failure in the months where the pipeline is thin.

The compensation is retention. A client who came back after nine years is worth more than four who never come back, and your own stories already prove you know how to earn that.

body_sections.heading: What the mark has to survive
body_sections.prose:
Stamped into metal, burned into wood, embroidered on a jacket, and legible at the size of a thumbnail on a phone. That list rules out anything with fine detail, gradients or more than two weights.

It also rules out the house silhouette, which every builder in the category already uses and which stops meaning anything at small sizes.

groups.label: Directions to brief
items: The joint. A mark built from a single visible connection, drawn the way a real joint is cut.
The stamp. A maker's mark that reads as ownership rather than as a company.
The level line. A single horizontal that sits exactly true, so any tilt in use reads as a mistake.

groups.label: Anti-patterns to hand the designer
items: No house silhouette. The category is saturated with it.
No hammer, no nail, no hard hat.
No gradient. It will not survive the metal stamp.

body_sections.heading: The sound of it
body_sections.prose:
Short sentences. Concrete nouns. A number wherever a number is available, because a number is the fastest proof that someone actually did the work.

No adjectives doing a verb's job. If the sentence needs stunning, beautiful or exceptional to carry it, the sentence has not earned its claim and should be rewritten around what was actually done.

body_sections.heading: The lexicon
body_sections.prose:
Use the words of the trade, unexplained. Mortise, reveal, plumb, scribe. A client who does not know them learns them, and learning them is part of why they trust you.

Never use the words of the brochure. Bespoke, artisan, curated and passion are all borrowed from someone else's category and they make specific work sound generic.

body_sections.heading: The ghostwriter test
body_sections.prose:
Three questions on any sentence before it ships. Did something actually happen in it. Could a competitor have written it. Is there a number available that you left out.

A sentence that fails any of the three gets rewritten around what was done, not deleted. Deleting is how a voice goes quiet; rewriting is how it gets specific.

groups.label: Write by these mechanics
items: Open with the material or the measurement. e.g. Forty-one feet of white oak, milled from two trees on the property.
One claim per sentence. e.g. The stair is oak. It was cut on site. It took nine days.
Replace an adjective with a number wherever one exists. e.g. Not a long project. A fourteen-month project.
Name what went wrong before naming what went right. e.g. We lost three weeks to the footing. Then it moved.
End on the object, not on the feeling. e.g. The bench is still there.

groups.label: Words and phrases we use
items: Mortise, reveal, plumb, scribe. Trade words, unexplained, because learning them is part of the trust.
On site. It locates the work in a place rather than in a process.
Milled. It names a step a volume builder skips.

groups.label: Words and phrases we never use
items: Bespoke. Borrowed from tailoring and worn out.
Artisan. It describes a price, not a practice.
Passionate. Every contractor says it, which makes it worth nothing.

always: Open with what was done, not what it felt like

body_sections.heading: What this reading is
body_sections.prose:
Your foundation is more decided than it feels. Four of the six sections are forced by your own answers and did not need a judgement call from the system.

Two are not, and both of those are commercial rather than creative. That is the pattern worth knowing about yourself.

body_sections.heading: The contradiction
body_sections.prose:
You want the work to speak for itself and you want to charge above the volume builders. Those pull against each other, because a price premium has to be argued and work that speaks for itself does not argue.

One of them leads. Until you choose which, the writing will keep hedging.

groups.label: Decided, and here is what decided it
items: The archetype is the Creator. Three stories, one shape, no counterexample.
The palette comes from materials. Your sensescape never once named equipment colour.
The client is someone let down before. You described them without being asked to.
Subcontracted finish work is out. You refused it twice, unprompted.

data_blocks.title: Still open, ranked by what they block

items.label: Whether the price is argued or implied
items.rationale: You want the work to speak for itself and you want a premium. A premium has to be argued. Nothing you answered chooses between them.

items.label: Who you turn down
items.rationale: You named an anti-brand but never an anti-client. Every project you described could plausibly be taken.

items.label: What the second crew changes
items.rationale: The refusal to subcontract finish work is load-bearing. Nothing in the foundation says what happens to it at twice the volume.
